meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The secret is to work less as individuals and more as a team. As a coach, I play not my eleven best, but my best eleven'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to Knute Rockne everywhere — but the earliest source we can find is a 1994 book, and no newspaper of his lifetime records the line.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1888–1931 · Notre Dame head coach, 105–12–5 across thirteen seasons
answer.sourceLine: The line is credited to Rockne in essentially every quotation collection, and it matches how he actually ran a team. What is missing is a source from his lifetime. Wikiquote ↗ lists it in its sourced section but traces it only to Jess Gibson’s Coaching Champions: The Privilege of Mentoring (1994), page 160 — sixty-three years after Rockne died. We could not push it back any further. Rockne’s own coaching manual, which we did read in full, uses the phrase “best eleven” and makes the teamwork argument — but not in these words. So this page stops at attributed.

source.excerpt: The secret is to work less as individuals and more as a team. As a coach, I play not my eleven best, but my best eleven.
trail: Wikiquote’s Rockne page ↗ places the line in its sourced section, but the source it gives is Jess Gibson, Coaching Champions: The Privilege of Mentoring (1994), p. 160 — a mentoring book published sixty-three years after Rockne’s death, not a document from his lifetime.

A full-text search of the Library of Congress’s Chronicling America ↗ newspaper archive for the phrase “not my eleven best” returns zero results. Rockne was among the most quoted men in American sport; a line he used would be unusual to leave no trace in the press.

Two of Rockne’s own books are readable in full at the Internet Archive, and the epigram is in neither: The Four Winners (1925) ↗ and his coaching manual Coaching: The Way of the Winner ↗. The manual is the interesting one. Rockne does use the construction — writing of knowing “who your best eleven men are, the second best eleven, and the third best eleven” — in a passage arguing that men should play together “for the sake of team work”. The vocabulary and the principle are his. The sentence is not there.

That leaves one obvious gap: The Autobiography of Knute K. Rockne (1931) is held by the Internet Archive but lending-restricted, so we could not search it. If the epigram is anywhere in his own words, that is the likeliest place.
Quote Investigator has not examined this line, so there is no specialist finding to defer to here.
source.excerptNote: This is the wording as Wikiquote ↗ carries it, italics and all. We have found no earlier printing to compare it against.
source.rightsNote: We cannot state a rights status honestly, because we cannot name the work this sentence first appeared in. Rockne died in 1931 and anything he published himself would now be in the public domain in the United States — but the earliest printing we located is a 1994 book, which is not, and we have no evidence linking the wording to Rockne’s own pen. Treat the text as of unknown status rather than free to reuse.

author.name: Knute Rockne
author.heading: About Knute Rockne
author.bio: Knute Rockne (4 March 1888 – 31 March 1931) was born in Voss, Norway, and came to Notre Dame first as a player and then, from 1918, as head coach. He went 105–12–5 across thirteen seasons, helped popularise the forward pass, and wrote several books on coaching before dying in a plane crash at forty-three. He was quoted constantly in his lifetime and has been quoted far more since — which is why lines credited to him need checking.

context.heading: Why coaches keep repeating it
lead: The sentence is a compact statement of the thing Rockne was genuinely famous for. He rotated whole units rather than star individuals, sending in fresh elevens that had practised together — the “shock troops” approach that helped carry Notre Dame to a 105–12–5 record ↗ over thirteen seasons.
That fit is probably why nobody ever questioned the attribution. It sounds exactly like him, which is the condition under which quotes drift onto a famous name and stay there.
detailsBody: A newspaper report, programme note or interview from between 1918 and 1931 carrying the phrase would move this page to verified in a sentence. The likeliest remaining hiding place is The Autobiography of Knute K. Rockne (1931), which the Internet Archive holds but lends rather than serves, so we could not search it. His two openly readable books have been searched and do not contain it.
If you have one, the page will be updated — provenance here is meant to be revisable, not decorative.
context.pull: It sounds exactly like him — which is precisely when a quote needs checking, not when it needs believing.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote lists this quote and cites Jess Gibson, Coaching Champions: The Privilege of Mentoring (1994), p. 160.
A Chronicling America full-text search for "not my eleven best" returns zero results.
The phrase does not appear in the full text of Rockne’s The Four Winners (1925).
Rockne lived 1888-1931, coached Notre Dame 1918-1930 to a 105-12-5 record, and authored several books including Coaching: The Way of the Winner (1925).
Archive.org holds Rockne’s Coaching: The Way of the Winner (1929 printing), creator "Knute K. Rockne".

Rockne’s Coaching: The Way of the Winner is served in full text by the Internet Archive and contains "who your best eleven men are, the second best eleven, and the third best eleven" in a passage stating men "should play together for the sake of team work", but does not contain the epigram.
